skript.thema: Claude Code token overhead before building a game

teile.name: Hook
teile.text: You open Claude Code, type nothing, and 33,000 tokens vanish. Check your token baseline first. One test measured roughly 33,000 tokens before the prompt arrived.
teile.szene: Original painted open-world-game poster style: a black-haired man in a black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses sits at a dim desk, frowning at a laptop's glow, medium shot, neon city night behind him.

teile.name: Comparison
teile.text: That's system prompt, tool schemas and scaffolding. OpenCode used about 7,000 for the same reply. Real projects add more, though.
teile.szene: Original painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses presenter in a leather jacket weighs a tall stack of glowing blocks against a small stack on a workshop bench, side-lit, medium shot, urban loft setting.

teile.name: Instruction file
teile.text: A 72KB instruction file adds roughly 20,000 tokens per request. Five modest MCP servers add 5,000 to 7,000 more.
teile.szene: Original painted game-poster style: the presenter in black leather jacket and cyan glasses stacks heavy glowing crates onto a growing pile beside a rooftop terminal, close-medium shot, dusk orange light.

teile.name: Question
teile.text: A working setup can sit 75,000 to 85,000 tokens deep before you type a word. Does Claude Code always cost more?
teile.szene: Original painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses presenter stands before a towering wall of glowing crates in a night alley, looking up with a wary expression, low-angle medium shot, teal and amber light.

teile.name: Twist
teile.text: Not always. On the first model, one multi-step task totaled less, because Claude Code batches tool calls into fewer requests.
teile.szene: Original painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses presenter raises an eyebrow, then smiles, as many small parcels slide into a few large boxes on a conveyor, medium shot, warm street light.

teile.name: Reversal
teile.text: A newer model reversed it: roughly 298,000 tokens against OpenCode's 133,000. Budget the baseline, then watch the session.
teile.szene: Original painted game-poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses watches two runners at a city track, one starting with a heavy backpack, wide shot, cool blue twilight.

teile.name: Ending
teile.text: Planning your game? Like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Original painted game-poster style: the presenter in black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses grins and sketches a game idea on a whiteboard in a bright studio, medium shot, warm light.

Claude Code changelog - Claude Code Docs
Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt
Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
This page is generated from the CHANGELOG.md on GitHub . Longer releases are grouped by type of change, with long lists of improvements and bug fixes collapsed.
Run claude --version to check your installed version.
Added /claude-api api-version to move Claude API code to API version 2026-10-21
Added the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event for each tool call a permission rule, auto mode, a safety check, a hook or the sandbox stopped, prompted or sent back
[VSCode] Added a notice on the microphone button when voice dictation stops by itself (15 seconds without recognized speech, or the 2-minute limit), saying why and that the text so far is kept
[Code Review] Added @claude review stop (also off and pause ) to Code Review, ending an @claude review always subscription on a pull request without starting a new review
Changed the notice Claude gets when the WebSearch budget is used up to also tell it not to query search engines in a browser or through computer use
Changed the axScreenReader setting and CLAUDE_AX_SCREEN_READER in a settings env block to apply only from user, managed or --settings settings (since 2.1.305)
Self-hosted runner: Changed checkout hooks to be stopped after 30 minutes by default, failing the session’s setup; if yours needs longer, raise --checkout-hook-timeout-min or set it to 0
Self-hosted runner: Changed the certificate file built for Anthropic-managed git to filter its trusted certificates as the CLI does; a [runner:warn] line gives the number left out
[VSCode] Changed the “still open somewhere else” notice to also cover a Claude process left over from an extension restart, which usually ends on its own within about 10 minutes
[VSCode] Changed voice dictation to filter its trusted certificates as the CLI does
[VSCode] Changed the extension’s own requests to filter their trusted certificates as the CLI does, and to trust the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS file named in the environment or in user settings
Improved recovery from unparseable tool calls: Claude Code now retries the call up to twice before ending the turn with an error
Improved fork subagents launched together: each is now told which launch is its own, so forks are much less likely to try to start each other’s work
Improved browser sign-in: the success page now appears as soon as sign-in completes, without waiting for your account profile to load
Improved web search errors in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions: a search refused with a 403 that gives a reason now shows that reason instead of a generic “Authentication error”
Improved the time to the first reply in cloud sessions when one of the desktop app’s MCP servers can’t connect
Improved Remote Control connect time for sessions whose transcript contains large pasted images or PDF reads
Fixed requests failing with a model-not-found error when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT is set and the model is an alias with the [1m] suffix, such as opus[1m]
Fixed the prompt-caching-scope beta header being sent behind custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL gateways and on Foundry, where it has no effect
Fixed MCP servers showing “needs authentication” in claude -p on macOS while the login keychain was locked; they now say why, and the next run after an unlock connects without a new sign-in
Fixed MCP servers being reported as timed out, and staying failed in headless runs, when a macOS or Linux computer went to sleep while they were connecting
Fixed HTTP MCP tool calls being sent twice when the connection closed mid-call; only read-only or idempotent tools are now retried
Fixed a turn sometimes starting without an SDK MCP server’s latest tools when a background task was running
Fixed some “Autocompact is thrashing” errors in turns that read many PDF pages, images or other large tool results
Fixed /autocompact in cloud sessions going back to the default window after the session restarted
Fixed a conversation cleared with /clear sometimes coming back when a cloud or self-hosted runner session restarted
Fixed CLAUDE_STREAM_FIRST_BYTE_TIMEOUT_MS being ignored in Claude apps gateway sessions
Fixed telemetry from Claude Desktop sessions behind a Claude apps gateway being rejected when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS is set
Fixed /permissions > Recently denied not showing the denied shell command, and auto mode’s local classifier ignoring an approval from there when it checks a retried command; approving a row now names the command, not its description
Fixed /help and the / command menu showing long model-facing descriptions for bundled skills such as /claude-api instead of their short descriptions
Fixed subagent transcripts recording placeholder token usage and an empty stop reason for streamed responses
Fixed model switches through the Agent SDK’s setModel() , and apps built on it, being refused when the API took more than 5 seconds to confirm the model; Claude Code now waits up to 15 seconds
Fixed a background command stopped through a connected app (such as the desktop app archiving an idle session) being reported to Claude as stopped by the user; the notice now names its output file
Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions reporting a tool error when a site answered with a 4xx status or a robots.txt refusal; it is now a normal result, as in local sessions
Fixed write tools on a directly configured GitHub MCP server showing a form that closed without creating anything in the desktop app’s Code tab
Fixed Artifact tool reads failing with a connection reset when the server had closed a reused connection
Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions with --use-anthropic-git-proxy committing a .claude/settings.local.json left in the clone by an earlier session
Self-hosted runner: Fixed archiving or requeueing a session, or stopping the runner, during its checkout hook leaving the hook’s processes running and the runner’s slot held

belege.name: Claude Code sends 33k tokens before reading the prompt; OpenCode sends 7k
belege.text:
Discussed on Hacker News (706 points, 2026-07-12).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Claude Code Sends 4.7x More Tokens Than OpenCode Before Reading Your Prompt | Systima Blog

We put Claude Code and OpenCode on the same model, the same machine, and the same tasks, then examined everything sent and received.

No spam. Unsubscribe at any time.
When we asked both harnesses for a one-line reply, Claude Code used roughly 33,000 tokens of system prompt, tool schemas, and injected scaffolding before the prompt even arrived. OpenCode used about 7,000.
Claude Code is far more cache inefficient:
OpenCode's request prefix was byte-identical in every run we captured; it paid to cache its payload once per session and read it back for pennies.
Claude Code on the other hand re-wrote tens of thousands of prompt-cache tokens mid-session, run after run, and on the same task wrote up to 54x more cache tokens than OpenCode .
Cache writes of course are billed at a premium, which accounted for the usage dashboard climbing when using Claude Code.
A production repository's 72KB instruction (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) file adds another (avg) 20,000 tokens to every single request. Five modest MCP servers add 5,000 to 7,000 more. By the time a real working setup sends its first request, it is 75,000 to 85,000 tokens deep before the user has typed a word.
A small task that cost 121,000 tokens done directly cost 513,000 tokens when fanned out to two subagents. This is because each subagent is its own agent that re-reads its own system prompt and tools on every turn it takes, so a fan-out multiplies the number of full baselines in flight.
Having said that, the parent ingests only each subagent's returned result, not its whole transcript.
We found one result in favour of Claude Code:
On a multi-step task Claude Code's whole-task total came out lower than OpenCode's, because it batches tool calls into fewer requests while OpenCode re-pays its smaller baseline turn after turn. The meter starts higher; how the session unfolds decides who spends more. That advantage held on the first model we tested; re-run on a newer one, the same task took twice the requests and cost roughly 298,000 tokens against OpenCode's 133,000.
Every finding above was cross-checked on a second model family. The pattern held, with one nuance we cover below.
The rest of this post shows how we measured all of this at the API boundary, where the tokens go, and what prompt caching does and does not save you.
Every token of harness payload is a token of working context you cannot spend on your task.
If you operate agentic AI in production, particularly under the EU AI Act where Article 12 expects you to log and understand your system's behaviour, "what does my agent actually send" is a question you should be able to answer with data.
We spliced a logging proxy between each harness and the model endpoint. harness (Claude Code / OpenCode)
→ logging proxy (captures request payloads + response usage)
The proxy records two things per request. The first is the exact JSON payload the harness emitted, meaning the system blocks, tool schemas, and messages. The second is the usage block the API returned, covering input tokens, cache writes, cache reads, and output tokens.
The payload capture is ground truth for what the harness sends. The usage block is ground truth for what was metered.
Harnesses. Claude Code 2.1.207 and OpenCode 1.17.18, both pinned to claude-sonnet-4-5 , July 2026. A reduced matrix (the floor, the cache task, and the multi-step task) was later re-run pinned to claude-fable-5 ; where the model changed the result, we say so inline.
Baseline isolation. Fresh config directories with no MCP servers, no user settings, and no memory; an empty workspace with no instruction files; permissions bypassed. Multiplier lanes then add one variable at a time.
Tasks. T1 says " Reply with exactly: OK " and isolates fixed overhead (three runs per harness). T2 reads a seeded file and summarises it. T3 is a write-run-test-fix loop against FizzBuzz plus a checker script.
Quality check. A separate ten-lane benchmark, five runs per harness against a seeded, hash-verified test suite, scored pass rates alongside token cost; reported in the quality section.
Zero-tools variant. Claude Code with --tools "" and OpenCode with "tools": {"*": false} , separating system prompt from tool schema weight.
One full disclosure note before the numbers:
Our traffic passes through Meridian , a local gateway that bridges the Claude Code SDK to a standard Anthropic endpoint so a Claude Max subscription can drive third-party tools. It wraps every request in the SDK's own envelope, a constant we measured at roughly 6,200 tokens on the Sonnet path and 3,500 on the Fable path with bare calibration requests and subtracted from every metered figure below.
Payload-level figures come from the captured request bodies, which the gateway cannot affect, and are exact.
Character-to-token conversion for component estimates uses each harness's own measured ratio of 4.1 to 4.4 characters per token, derived from cold-cache anchors where the metered write equals the full payload, rather than a generic heuristic.
The fixed overhead of saying OK
The task was 22 characters. Here is what each harness sent with it on its first request.
OpenCode's request is close to minimal. There is one system block that opens with " You are OpenCode, the best coding agent on the planet ", plus ten classic coding tools, plus the user's prompt as the only content.
Claude Code's request is a platform bootstrap. The 27 tools include the coding core plus an entire background-agent and orchestration suite, from CronCreate and Monitor to the Task family, worktree management, and

belege.name: Claude Code uses Bun written in Rust now
belege.text:
Discussed on Hacker News (608 points, 2026-07-19).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Claude Code uses Bun written in Rust now
Sponsored by: Teleport — AI agents (and sub-agents they spawn) are given the same access as humans, but they never sleep. Learn how to monitor and constrain their behavior with isolated ephemeral trusted runtimes.
In Rewriting Bun in Rust Jarred Sumner made the following claim:
Claude Code v2.1.181 (released June 17th) and later use the Rust port of Bun. Startup got 10% faster on Linux but otherwise, barely anyone noticed. Boring is good.
I decided to have a poke at my own Claude Code installation to see if I could find evidence that it was using Bun written in Rust.
I found these two commands convincing:
strings ~/.local/bin/claude | grep -m1 'Bun v1'
For me this outputs Bun v1.4.0 (macOS arm64) . The most recent release of Bun on GitHub is currently v1.3.14 from May 12th, so that v1.4.0 version number in Claude supports them shipping a preview of a not-yet-released Bun version.
( Update : The Rust version has been released as Bun canary - running bun upgrade --canary will install this release .)
strings ~/.local/bin/claude | grep -Eo 'src/[[:alnum:]_./-]+\.rs'
This outputs a list of 563 filenames , starting with these:
It looks like Bun in Rust is indeed being run in production across millions of different devices. Like Jarred said, "Boring is good".
Update : Here's a neat trick from Ajan Raj :
Here's the commit from May 17th that updated the version in package.json to 1.4.0. That version hasn't been changed since then, but also hasn't yet made it into a tagged release outside of canary .
